Spirit, I hear your words. Our granaries are full enough to see us through the season, yet we have spare grain. I will set aside a handful of bundles—enough for a few weeks of our folk—to send to the Wewush people. I will ask a few hunters and a keeper of the fire to carry it, that the aid may reach them before the lean winter comes. May the spirits watch our trade and keep both villages fed.

Spirit, your words I hear. Our stores are full and the fields will give again when the wheat is sown. The folk of Wewush suffer hunger, and it is right to share what we have. I will set aside a portion of our grain, enough for a week’s feed, and send it with a few of our hunters who travel to the coast. In return I will ask that they keep the road between us clear and bring any news of game or fire‑stone they find. Let the spirits guide them safely home.

Spirit of the wind, I hear your voice upon the thatch.  
I have felt the gusts sweep the fields and hear them howl through the trees, but I have not spoken to the wind as a being.  

Tell me, if you are the wind, what does your moving favor ask of us?  
Do you bring a warning of storm, or a blessing of rain for the seeds?  
And if you are but the breath of the sky, how might we honor the breath that steadies our fire and lifts our smoke?

Spirit, I hear your voice. Our stores are full—enough grain to feed our folk many moons, and our stores of fish, meat and hide stand ready. The hunger of the folk at Wewush is a weight upon my heart, and giving grain would sow goodwill and keep the spirit of sharing alive.

I will set aside a modest sack of grain, enough to ease their need but not to endanger our own winter. A few of our able adults shall escort it, and the rest of the work shall continue as ordered. If the winds bring word that they repay us in kind, we shall welcome it; if not, we shall have done what the spirits ask without risking our own hearth.
